```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = TRUE)
```

This is a reference article about the two catch tables `{obus}` derives from the
DATRAS HL record — `HL_length` and `HL_summary` — and about the parts of the
ICES exchange format that decide what numbers come out of them. It describes
what the package does now. It does not propose changes to it.

Every claim below is either a quotation from an ICES document or a measurement
of the archive, and the measurements are given as code you can run. The
examples read the published tables directly, so they need nothing but the
package:

```{r}
library(obus)
library(dplyr)
```

The article is in two parts. **Part I** is what `HL_length` and `HL_summary`
are, what they answer, and why they are worth using instead of the raw record.
**Part II** is the conventions and contradictions in the exchange format that
decide what numbers come out of them, ordered by how far each one can move a
result.

**What this is arguing for is the tables, not the package.** `HL_length` and
`HL_summary` are the calculation nearly every DATRAS analysis performs before
it does anything else, and the right home for them is ICES's own product
suite, next to CPUEL — computed once, centrally, and served to everyone. Not
re-implemented once per institute, once per language, once per working group,
each version quietly differing from the others in exactly the places Part II
catalogues.

[`{obus}`](https://github.com/einarhjorleifsson/obus) is a reference
implementation of that idea and a demonstration that it holds for the whole
archive rather than part of it. Every rule it applies is quoted from an ICES
document below; every figure is reproducible from the published archive with
the code shown. If ICES served these two tables, this package would not need
to exist — and that would be the better outcome. The nearest thing to a proof
of the proposal is that [CPUEL itself can be rebuilt from
`HL_length`](#building-cpuel-from-hl_length), which is shown below.

Read the balance right. [`{obus}`](https://github.com/einarhjorleifsson/obus)
applies ICES's own procedures throughout, and each of them is a document you
can open:

- the **raising steps** come from the index-calculation procedures —
  [`Indices_Calculation_Steps_IBTS`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/Indices_Calculation_Steps_IBTS.pdf)
  [@ices2022ibtsindices] and
  [`Indices_Calculation_Steps_BITS`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/Indices_Calculation_Steps_BITS.pdf)
  [@ices2013bitsindices];
- the **field meanings** come from the
  [field descriptions](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/DATRAS_Field_descriptions_and_example_file_December2025.xlsx)
  [@ices2026fielddesc], and the worked Example file in the same workbook;
- the **field names** come from ICES's own crosswalk — the
  [`getDatrasFieldList`](https://datras.ices.dk/WebServices/DATRASWebService.asmx/getDatrasFieldList)
  web service and the
  [New Headers lookup](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/DATRAS_NewHeaders_Lookup_Dec2024.xlsx)
  [@ices2024newheaders].

For most of the format that is the whole story, so it is not written about
here. The later sections concentrate on the small number of places where two
ICES statements pull in different directions, or where the format says nothing
and `{obus}` had to choose. Their prominence in this article is not their
prominence in the data.

# Part I. What the two tables are for

## Why these two tables exist

An HL record is a **submission**, not a catch. What a country sends ICES for
one haul is a set of length rows: a length class, the number of fish measured
in that class, the raising factor relating the measured sub-sample to the
whole catch, and — repeated on every row — the totals for that species
category in number and weight. Taken at face value a length row says "*n* fish
measured", not "*n* fish caught".

Getting from one to the other is the same short list of steps for every survey
in the archive:

- raise the measured numbers by the sub-sampling factor;
- turn the length class into a length, in known units;
- decide what to do when the raising factor is missing, or the haul lasted no
  time at all;
- avoid adding up a total the submitter repeated across sex or category rows.

Nearly every DATRAS analysis begins there, and they are the same steps every
time.

### `HL_length` is CPUEL, generalised

ICES already publishes this table. It is called **CPUEL** — catch per unit
effort at length: numbers per hour by haul, species and length class,
[@ices2021units] — and it is the natural starting point for length-based work,
computed centrally so that nobody downstream has to raise a sub-sample again.

It covers **8 of the archive's 29 surveys**:

```{r}
duckdbfs::open_dataset("https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/CPUEL.parquet") |>
  distinct(Survey) |> count()                     #> 8

dr_con("HH") |> distinct(Survey) |> count()       #> 29
```

`HL_length` is that same table for all 29. Where the two snapshots are of the
same vintage it reproduces CPUEL on effectively every haul and count that can
be fairly compared — 98.5% of CPUEL's rows and 94.1% of its counts across
5.5 million records, and 97.4% of counts for six of the eight surveys once
BITS and SWC-IBTS are set aside. BITS differs for reasons that are understood
and documented here ([D20](#d20)–[D22](#d22): a cod-only gear conversion CPUEL
applies and `{obus}` does not, and a length grid CPUEL does not preserve);
SWC-IBTS is unexplained. The full comparison is a chapter of its own in the
`datrasdoodle2` book.

Two differences run the other way:

- **Sex.** CPUEL carries `sex` as `NA` on every survey. `HL_length` keeps
  `SpeciesSex` wherever it was recorded, and some surveys record it heavily —
  everything on ROCKALL, 64% of SWC-IBTS, 76% of EVHOE.
- **Zero rows.** Roughly half of CPUEL's rows are explicit zeros; `HL_length`
  adds none. That is not an oversight but the reason it generalises. A zero
  only means *none caught* if you know the species was in scope for that haul,
  and settling that universe is a survey-by-survey judgement. Leaving it out
  is what lets the same function work identically on all 29 surveys instead of
  stopping at eight — and it leaves the choice of universe with you.

None of that is a complaint about CPUEL. ICES's Data Centre builds and
maintains real, working products — CPUE by length, by age, catch weight,
abundance indices — computed centrally so downstream tools call straight
through. That is the right shape, and it is the shape this article is asking
for more of. The argument is narrower than it may sound: the length-frequency
half of that suite does not need the zero-fill question answered first, so it
can be built for every survey.

### Building CPUEL from `HL_length` {#building-cpuel-from-hl_length}

The clearest way to see that these are the same table is to build one from the
other. CPUEL's payload is numbers per hour by haul, species and length class —
`.id`, `aphia`, `length_mm`, `n_hour` — with `sex` empty throughout.
`HL_length` is finer than that in three ways it keeps on purpose (sex,
development stage and length measurement type), so CPUEL is one aggregation
away:

```{r}
cpuel_like <- dr_con("HL_length") |>
  filter(Survey == "NS-IBTS", Year == 2023, Quarter == 1) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, length_mm) |>
  summarise(n_hour = sum(n_hour, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

Set that against ICES's own file for the same hauls:

```{r}
cpuel <- duckdbfs::open_dataset("https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/CPUEL.parquet") |>
  filter(Survey == "NS-IBTS", Year == 2023, Quarter == 1, n_hour > 0) |>
  select(.id, Valid_Aphia = aphia, length_mm, cpuel = n_hour)

cpuel_like |>
  inner_join(cpuel, by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "length_mm")) |>
  summarise(cells = n(),
            agree = sum(ifelse(abs(n_hour - cpuel) < 0.001, 1, 0)))
```

```
  cells agree
  40027 38607        # 96.45% agree to a thousandth of a fish per hour
```

Over the 317 hauls both sides cover, the rebuild matches **96.6% of CPUEL's
non-zero cells** and agrees with **96.45%** of those to a thousandth of a fish
per hour; the median ratio is exactly 1.000. A worked haul, three cod:

```{r}
cpuel_like |>
  inner_join(cpuel, by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "length_mm")) |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2023:1:DE:06NI:GOV:104:22", Valid_Aphia == 126436) |>
  arrange(length_mm)
```

```
  .id                               Valid_Aphia length_mm n_hour cpuel
  NS-IBTS:2023:1:DE:06NI:GOV:104:22      126436       410      2     2
  NS-IBTS:2023:1:DE:06NI:GOV:104:22      126436       470      2     2
  NS-IBTS:2023:1:DE:06NI:GOV:104:22      126436       580      2     2
```

The residual is accounted for and none of it is arithmetic. The two files are
independent downloads with their own calculation vintages, so a haul revised
on one side and not the other differs. On BITS two further, documented things
apply: CPUEL gear-standardises cod and nothing else ([D21](#d21)) and does not
always preserve the submitted length grid ([D22](#d22)) — both of which a
generalised product would have to decide about explicitly rather than inherit.

**The zero rows are the part that is not one aggregation away**, and
deliberately so. Half of CPUEL is explicit zeros — 5,874,543 of 11,774,468
rows, each carrying `length_mm = 0` — and they encode a judgement about which
species were in scope for a haul. Add them yourself and the judgement stays
yours:

```{r}
hauls   <- cpuel_like |> distinct(.id) |> collect()
species <- cpuel_like |> distinct(Valid_Aphia) |> collect()    # your universe, not ours

tidyr::crossing(hauls, species) |>
  left_join(collect(cpuel_like), by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia")) |>
  tidyr::replace_na(list(n_hour = 0, length_mm = 0))
```

On this one survey-quarter that turns 318 hauls and 141 species into 81,557
rows, 38,513 of them explicit zeros — the same roughly-half proportion CPUEL
carries, arrived at from a universe you chose rather than one you inherited.

That is the whole distance between `HL_length` and a CPUEL product covering
29 surveys rather than 8: one `group_by()`, plus a species universe that only a
survey group can properly set.

### Existing analyses run on them unchanged

A product also has to leave standing what is already built on the exchange
tables. So: starting from these two tables instead of the raw HL record, can
the usual chain still be run — numbers at length raised to the haul, summed to
total numbers and weight per haul, divided by swept area and carried through to
a stratified abundance index?

`data-raw/CHECK_datras_adapter.R` answers that against real numbers. It
assembles an object whose HL comes **only** from `HL_length` and `HL_summary`,
never from raw HL, runs [`{DATRAS}`](https://github.com/DTUAqua/DATRAS) and
`{DATRASextra}` on it unmodified, and compares with the same steps run on their
own bundled fixture — NS-IBTS 2020–2023, quarters 1 and 3, dab (*Limanda
limanda*), 2,651 valid hauls. The adapter is about 60 lines: rename to the
legacy field names, add the five HH quantities the packages derive for
themselves, and reshape the two catch tables into the single HL frame they
expect. **No arithmetic on any number** — the raised number at length is
`n_haul` exactly as published.

| Step | Quantity | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| numbers at length, by length class | `N`, 41 classes | same classes, **max gap 0** over 108,691 cells |
| total numbers per haul | `HaulN` | **max gap 0** over 2,651 hauls |
| total weight per haul, from the length–weight lookup | `HaulWgt` | **max gap 0** |
| swept area | `SweptArea` | **max gap 0** |
| stratified abundance index, per hour, by statistical rectangle | index and CV | **identical** |

Eleven checks, no differences (re-run 2026-09-08). The last of them is the
figure a survey working group would report, and it comes out the same to every
digit:

```
  Year    index         cv
  2020 771.7314 0.07114170
  2021 712.8609 0.09926699
  2022 823.4249 0.06559173
  2023 739.3506 0.05788805
```

Two caveats. Species recorded in a haul but never measured enter through
`HL_summary`, carrying no length — which is how the exchange format carries
them, and what a species-richness count needs; a length table alone would lose
them. And **CA is out of scope**: `{obus}` derives no age table, so nothing
age-, maturity- or individual-weight-based is exercised.

Underneath sits the field-by-field comparison,
`data-raw/CHECK_datras_interop.R` — 25 checks, no differences, including the
raised number at length (max gap 2.3 × 10⁻¹³ over 24,960 cells) and the
measured number at length, `HLNoAtLngt`, against `n_measured` (max gap 0 over
16,196 cells).

### What that saves you downstream

`HL_length` and `HL_summary` exist so this is done once, the same way for the
whole archive, following ICES's own written procedure — and so that the hauls
where it cannot be done cleanly are visible rather than quietly absorbed.

Done by hand, none of those steps is hard, exactly. They are a lot of
bookkeeping to get right every time, and easy to get subtly wrong once — and a
species silently missing from a haul reads exactly like a species nobody ever
looked for. Everything downstream starts from the same table: length spectra,
abundance and biomass per haul, CPUE, stratified indices, species composition,
age–length keys. Getting the first step wrong once is getting it wrong
everywhere.

### One haul, from submission to catch at length

A single sprat record shows the whole shape of it. Fourteen length rows as
submitted:

```{r}
dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  dr_add_id() |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2020:1:DK:26D4:GOV:11:4", Valid_Aphia == 126425) |>
  select(LengthCode, LengthClass, NumberAtLength, SubsamplingFactor,
         SubsampledNumber, TotalNumber, SpeciesCategoryWeight) |>
  collect() |> 
  arrange(LengthClass) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

Four things have to happen before that is a catch at length:

- **The units have to be resolved.** `LengthCode` `.` declares `LengthClass` to
  be in millimetres, so 55 is 5.5 cm and the class is 1 mm wide.
- **The numbers have to be raised.** The six fish measured at 5.5 cm stand for
  6 × 11.312 = 67.9 fish in the catch.
- **The sub-sample is not the catch.** The 142 in `SubsampledNumber` is what
  went through the calipers, not what came aboard.
- **The total is written once but repeated everywhere.** `TotalNumber` 1606.3
  is one figure for the whole species in this haul, standing on all fourteen
  rows — add the column up and you have fourteen times the catch.

`HL_length` carries the raised numbers at length, in resolved units:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_length") |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2020:1:DK:26D4:GOV:11:4", Valid_Aphia == 126425) |>
  select(length_cm, accuracy, n_haul, n_hour, n_measured) |>
  arrange(length_cm)
```

```
  length_cm accuracy  n_haul n_measured
        5.5      0.1  67.872          6
        6.0      0.1 633.472         56
        6.5      0.1 463.792         41
        7.0      0.1 113.120         10
        7.5      0.1  11.312          1
          …        …       …          …
```

and `HL_summary` carries one row for the species in the haul, with the
reported total beside the reconstructed one:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2020:1:DK:26D4:GOV:11:4", Valid_Aphia == 126425) |>
  select(species, n_totalnumber, n_haul, n_measured, w_haul)
```

```
         species n_totalnumber   n_haul n_measured w_haul
  European sprat        1606.3 1606.304        142   3948
```

1606.3 against 1606.304: the reported total and the raised length frequencies
agree here to four thousandths of a fish, which is simply what a non-integer
raising factor applied to whole fish does. [Two routes to a catch
total](#two-routes-to-a-catch-total) is about the hauls where they do not
agree.

### What each table answers

| | `HL_length` | `HL_summary` |
|---|---|---|
| One row is | a species at one length class in one haul | a species in one haul |
| Which species | only those actually measured | every species recorded, measured or not |
| Numbers | `n_haul`, `n_hour` — raised; `n_measured` — as measured | `n_totalnumber`, `n_totalnumber_hour` — as reported; `n_haul` — reconstructed from the length frequencies; `n_measured` |
| Weight | — | `w_haul`, `w_hour` |
| Sex | `SpeciesSex` carried as reported | summarised as `p_females` |
| Rows | 14,001,605 | 2,291,457 |
| Reach for it for | length spectra, size-based indices, ALK inputs, length–weight work | abundance and biomass per haul, CPUE, species composition, stratified indices |

Both are published as parquet files and read lazily: ask for one survey, year
or species and only those rows are fetched, so a single haul can be inspected
without downloading the archive.

### Why two tables and not one

Two reasons, and both come from the data rather than from convenience.

**Most of a haul's species roster is not length-measured.** A haul's record
routinely includes species that were only counted in bulk, only weighed, or
only noted as present. 366,013 of `HL_summary`'s 2,291,457 rows — **16.0%** —
have no length rows behind them at all:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  anti_join(dr_con("HL_length") |> distinct(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity),
            by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "SpeciesValidity")) |>
  count()
```

Those species cannot appear in a length table, and giving them a placeholder
length row would invent a measurement that was never made. `HL_length` is
therefore the length-measured subset by construction, and `HL_summary` is the
full roster.

**Numbers and weights survive being split by sex differently.** `HL_length`
carries `SpeciesSex` as reported, because `NumberAtLength` is a genuine
per-sex count. `SpeciesCategoryWeight` is not reliably per-sex — DATRAS
repeats one weight across a species' sex rows — so a table split by sex would
state a weight that was never weighed. Keeping the two quantities in tables of
different shape is what lets each be right. This is worked through in [what
makes a row unique](#what-makes-a-row-unique) below.

### What makes a row unique {#what-makes-a-row-unique}

ICES states the record's identity in the field descriptions, four times over —
once each under `TotalNumber`, `SubsampledNumber`, `NumberAtLength` and
`SpeciesCategoryWeight` — and all four name the same five components, the

> unique combination of cruise haul, species, sex, devstage and subsampling
> category identifier

(the phrasing varies slightly between the four cells; the components do not).
So an HL record is identified by **haul × species × sex × `DevelopmentStage` ×
`SpeciesCategory`**, and the length rows add `LengthClass` and `LengthType`.
The two `{obus}` tables follow that, with the sub-sampling category summed away:

| Table | One row per |
|---|---|
| `HL_length` | `.id` × `Valid_Aphia` × `length_mm` × `length_cm` × `accuracy` × `LengthType` × `SpeciesSex` × `DevelopmentStage` × `SpeciesValidity` |
| `HL_summary` | `.id` × `Valid_Aphia` × `SpeciesValidity` |

Each is exactly unique there — no repeated combinations at all, over 14 million
rows — and at anything coarser it is not, so **add `n_haul` up rather than
assuming one row**:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_length") |>
  count(.id, Valid_Aphia, length_mm, length_cm, accuracy,
        LengthType, SpeciesSex, DevelopmentStage, SpeciesValidity) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  count()                                   #> 0
```

`LengthType` and `DevelopmentStage` are part of what makes a row unique, not
labels carried along, because ICES's record identity puts them there: one haul
can measure the same species at the same length under two measurement
conventions, or as both egg-bearing and unstaged, and each is its own count.
Over the 13,992,024 combinations at the coarser `.id` × `Valid_Aphia` ×
`length_mm` × `SpeciesSex` level, 5,611 split on `DevelopmentStage` (0.040%),
4,044 on `LengthType` (0.029%), and 15 each on `SpeciesValidity` and
`accuracy` (0.0001%). Rare — but each split is a separate count, and collapsing
one is silent. `DevelopmentStage` is the easiest to overlook, being `NA` for
99.8% of rows, and dropping it would add a berried record to an unstaged one.

That choice has one measurable cost, in [duplicated length
series](#duplicated-length-series) below.

### Why `HL_summary` is not split by sex

`HL_length` carries `SpeciesSex`; `HL_summary` does not. The asymmetry is
deliberate, and it is a property of the submissions rather than a limitation of
the package.

`NumberAtLength` is a genuine per-sex, per-length count, and — checked over the
whole archive — never repeats one placeholder value across a species' sex rows.
`TotalNumber` does: across the 212,497 haul × species records reporting more
than one sex (9.3% of 2,290,235), it varies genuinely by sex for 66% of them
and is a species-level figure written identically onto every sex row for the
other 34%. Per-sex arithmetic can tell those two apart, and `{obus}` does exactly
that (see [how `{obus}` resolves a repeated
`TotalNo`](#how-obus-deduplicates-totalno)).

`SpeciesCategoryWeight` has no comparable check, and its
repeats-versus-varies pattern tracks `TotalNumber`'s only about half the time.
Splitting `HL_summary` by sex would therefore misstate `w_haul` for an unknown
share of species with no way to flag which. Sex-specific *numbers* stay
available by adding up `HL_length`; sex-specific *weight* is not recoverable in
general. That is a property of the source data, not a gap in `{obus}`.

Sex codes are kept as reported — `"F"`, `"M"`, `"U"`, `"B"` or `NA`. `"B"`
(berried, egg-bearing) is not folded into `"F"`, and `"U"` (examined,
undetermined) stays distinct from `NA` (never examined). The female proportion
`HL_summary` publishes as `p_females` is one step away from `HL_length`:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_length") |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia) |>
  summarise(
    p_females = sum(n_haul[SpeciesSex %in% c("F", "B")]) /
                sum(n_haul[SpeciesSex %in% c("F", "M", "B")]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Do the derived tables still say what the submissions said?

Yes, and this is checked rather than assumed. Compared cell by cell against the
DATRAS R package's own `Count` [@kristensen2023datraspkg] across every species
and survey:

| | |
|---|---|
| haul × species × length cells compared | 13,214,965 |
| exact matches | 13,191,109 |
| cells differing by ≥ 0.5 fish | **0** |
| largest difference | 2.9 × 10⁻¹¹ (floating point) |
| in `HL_length` but not in raw HL | **0** |
| in raw HL but not in `HL_length` | 23,856 — every one where `n_haul` is `NA` |

Those 23,856 rows (0.18%) are the one deliberate difference: where the raising
factor is missing, DATRAS assumes 1 and `{obus}` returns `NA`, because ICES makes
the field mandatory. That is a choice, argued in [sub-sampling and the raising
factor](#sub-sampling-the-raising-factor-and-datatype), not an error.

The tables are faithful but they are **not lossless**. 13,957,390 of
`HL_length`'s 14,001,605 rows (99.68%) come from exactly one submitted HL row;
44,215 combine several, and there the raising factor (42,089 rows) and the
sub-sampling category (43,989 rows) are summed away. Also absent at this level:
`SubsampledNumber`, `SubsampleWeight`, per-category `SpeciesCategoryWeight`
(`w_haul` is summed to the species) and sex-specific weight.

### What to use instead, and when

| Question | Table |
|---|---|
| length spectra, numbers or biomass per haul, CPUE, stratified indices, species composition | `HL_length` + `HL_summary` |
| sub-sampling checks, anything per `SpeciesCategory`, per-category weights, provenance, rebuilding an exchange file | `dr_con("HL")` — the record layer, exactly as submitted plus `.id` |
| age, individual weight, maturity, age–length keys | `dr_con("CA")` — `{obus}` derives no CA table |

The first row is demonstrated rather than asserted — see [existing analyses run
on them unchanged](#existing-analyses-run-on-them-unchanged) above.

## Field names: two layers, both ICES's {#two-naming-layers}


Field names in this codebase come from two places — **both of them ICES's** —
and there is deliberately no third.

| Layer | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. ICES legacy exchange names** | The names the exchange file still carries, and the ones the older ICES documents quoted here use. | `HLNoAtLngt`, `SubFactor`, `CatIdentifier` |
| **2. ICES current names** | ICES's replacement names, published in the current field descriptions. What the raw parquet archive carries, and what every `{obus}` table carries too. | `NumberAtLength`, `SubsamplingFactor`, `SpeciesCategory` |

**The translation between the two layers is ICES's own, not this package's.**
ICES is renaming DATRAS's fields table by table, and publishes the
old-to-new pairs itself in two places: the `getDatrasFieldList` operation on
the DATRAS web service, which returns each current `FieldName` alongside the
`FieldNameOld` it was renamed from, and the *DATRAS New Headers Lookup*
spreadsheet of December 2024 [@ices2024newheaders], which carries the same
pairs in one sheet per record type. Layer 2 is therefore not a scheme `{opus}`
invented and `{obus}` adopted — it is ICES's own target naming, taken up ahead of
the migration's completion. The migration's progress is visible in the service:
HL has flipped, and `getHLdataNewHeaders` returns all 29 of its fields under
the current names, while HH, CA and LT are still served under legacy names
only.

The documentation has already moved ahead of the service: the current field
descriptions name every field in layer 2, so a reader working from ICES's
workbook and a reader working from the `{obus}` tables see the same column names.
Legacy names survive in four places:

- the exchange files themselves;
- the web-service operations that have not yet flipped;
- the older ICES documents quoted later in this article;
- and, in a handful of cells, the current descriptions' own prose — where
  formulas still read `TotalNo=SUM(HLNoAtLngt)` and *"If DataType is C,
  CatIdentifier is always 1"* beneath fields now called `TotalNumber` and
  `SpeciesCategory`.

Quotations below keep whatever names the quoted document uses.

**`{obus}` invents no field names.** `dr_con_raw("HL")` and `dr_con("HL_length")`
both carry `Valid_Aphia` and `SpeciesSex`, so a join between the raw archive and
a derived table needs no name mapping, and the crosswalk below describes every
column in every table.

A shorter `sex` column is a tempting simplification, and it is the wrong one.
ICES's legacy `Sex` maps to `SpeciesSex` in HL but to `IndividualSex` in CA —
two genuinely different measurements, one a property of a length-frequency
record and the other of an individual fish. A single `sex` column flattens
them.

### The legacy-to-current crosswalk

The mapping is neither hand-authored here nor taken from ICES's published
lists on trust. `{opus}` checks every pair ICES publishes against the field names
the corresponding operation actually returns, keeps what survives
(`opus::op_datras_field_list()`), reduces that to a collision-checked 1:1 map
(`opus::op_datras_rename_crosswalk()`), and embeds the result in the raw
parquet footer. `{obus}` reads it back from the same file as the data, so it
cannot describe a different vintage than the data it accompanies:

```{r}
opus::op_crosswalk("HL")
```

```
          old_name              new_name
        RecordType          RecordHeader
            Survey                Survey
           Quarter               Quarter
           Country               Country
              Ship              Platform
              Gear                  Gear
         SweepLngt           SweepLength
            GearEx        GearExceptions
          DoorType              DoorType
              StNo           StationName
            HaulNo            HaulNumber
              Year                  Year
      SpecCodeType       SpeciesCodeType
          SpecCode           SpeciesCode
           SpecVal       SpeciesValidity
               Sex            SpeciesSex
           TotalNo           TotalNumber
     CatIdentifier       SpeciesCategory
            NoMeas      SubsampledNumber
         SubFactor     SubsamplingFactor
            SubWgt       SubsampleWeight
       CatCatchWgt SpeciesCategoryWeight
          LngtCode            LengthCode
         LngtClass           LengthClass
        HLNoAtLngt        NumberAtLength
          DevStage      DevelopmentStage
       LenMeasType            LengthType
 DateofCalculation     DateofCalculation
       Valid_Aphia           Valid_Aphia
```

29 rows — two more than either ICES list. Neither `getDatrasFieldList` nor the
December 2024 lookup documents HL's `DateofCalculation` or `Valid_Aphia` under
any name, though both are real fields that `getHLdata` and
`getHLdataNewHeaders` alike return; they appear here unrenamed, which is what
those two operations show them to be.

Check names against this output rather than from memory. Most pairs
are guessable; at least one is not — **`LenMeasType` maps to `LengthType`**,
which is easy to mistake for a length *unit* field when it is a measurement
*convention* field. `Sex` → `SpeciesSex` is the pair worth memorising, because ICES's one legacy
`Sex` splits across two current names — `SpeciesSex` in HL and
`IndividualSex` in CA — so it is the clearest case of why the crosswalk is
per table rather than global.

## The haul identifier, `.id`

`.id` is an `{obus}` construct; ICES has no such field. It is the eight fields
ICES's own exchange tables use to key a haul, concatenated with `:` —

`Survey : Year : Quarter : Country : Platform : Gear : StationName : HaulNumber`

— for example `"BITS:1991:1:DE:06S1:H20:33:28"`. `NA` fields (most often
`StationName`) are skipped rather than rendered as the literal string `"NA"`,
matching the convention the published archive already uses. When every field
is `NA` the result is `NA`, not the empty string, because an empty string
would collide every such row onto one identifier.

`dr_add_id()` accepts only the current names. A legacy-named table must be
renamed first (`opus::op_rename()`); `Ship`, `StNo` and `HaulNo` are not
handled.

# Part II. What stands in the way

## What ICES provides, and what counts as evidence

DATRAS is a well-specified format, and most of what follows is only possible
because of that. ICES publishes:

- a **field-by-field description** of every record type, with data types,
  widths and mandatory flags;
- **a worked Example file inside the same workbook**, which settles arithmetic
  that prose leaves ambiguous;
- the **index-calculation procedures** its own products are built from;
- a **units specification** for those products;
- **the products themselves** — CPUEL among them — so an outside
  reimplementation can be checked against ICES's own numbers;
- a **machine-readable web service** reporting each table's real field names
  and types;
- a **working-group process** — IBTSWG, WGDG — that reviews the format and
  minutes the result.

Few survey-data formats of this age hand an outside implementation that many
independent ways to check itself.

That redundancy is what makes the [discrepancy
register](#register-of-cross-document-discrepancies) below possible at all.
Nearly every entry in it was found by checking ICES against ICES: a formula
against the Example file in the same workbook, a recipe against the product
ICES ships from it, a field list against the service that serves it. A format
documented in one place only would yield a shorter register and worse data.

**Only ICES's own published documents count as evidence here.** For this
package that means the primary sources kept in
`~/R/Pakkar/imbus/DATRAS/external/`, principally:

| Source | Short name used below |
|---|---|
| [`DATRAS_Field_descriptions_and_example_file_December2025.xlsx`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/DATRAS_Field_descriptions_and_example_file_December2025.xlsx) [@ices2026fielddesc] | the field descriptions, or "the spreadsheet" |
| [`DATRAS_FAQs`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/DATRAS_FAQs.pdf) v3.0, August 2014 [@ices2014datrasfaqs] | the FAQ |
| [`Indices_Calculation_Steps_IBTS`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/Indices_Calculation_Steps_IBTS.pdf) [@ices2022ibtsindices], [`Indices_Calculation_Steps_BITS`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/Indices_Calculation_Steps_BITS.pdf) [@ices2013bitsindices] | the index procedures |
| [`DATRAS_dataproducts_units` v3.1](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/3.1.DATRAS_dataproducts_units.pdf) [@ices2021units] — [v3.0](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/DATRAS_dataproducts_units.pdf) [@ices2017units] only where the two differ | the units specification |
| [`DATRAS_NewHeaders_Lookup_Dec2024.xlsx`](https://www.ices.dk/data/Documents/DATRAS/DATRAS_NewHeaders_Lookup_Dec2024.xlsx) [@ices2024newheaders] | the New Headers lookup |
| [`WKDATR13`](https://doi.org/10.17895/ices.pub.21655439) (ICES CM 2013/SSGESST:05) [@ices2013wkdatr] | the 2013 data-review workshop |
| [`WKABSENS` 2021](https://doi.org/10.17895/ices.pub.8299) [@ices2021wkabsens] | the absence-record workshop |
| IBTSWG reports, [2022](https://doi.org/10.17895/ices.pub.20502828), [2024](https://doi.org/10.17895/ices.pub.28562888) and 2025 meetings [@ices2022ibtswg; @ices2025ibtswg; @ices2026ibtswg] | IBTSWG 2022, IBTSWG 2024, IBTSWG 2025 |
| `Reporting_Pseudo_Category_To_DATRAS` (Vaishav, 19/01/2021, marked *Draft*, unpublished) [@vaishav2021pseudocat] | the pseudo-category memo |

One further primary source is live rather than filed: the DATRAS web service
itself, whose
[`getDatrasFieldList`](https://datras.ices.dk/WebServices/DATRASWebService.asmx/getDatrasFieldList)
operation publishes the field-name mapping used in [Field names: two layers,
both ICES's](#two-naming-layers), and whose
[per-table operations](https://datras.ices.dk/WebServices/DATRASWebService.asmx)
report the field names each table really carries.

**This article describes the format as it currently stands.** The field
descriptions are a living workbook, revised periodically, and the December
2025 vintage is the one quoted throughout unless a passage says otherwise.
Superseded vintages are cited in two situations only: where the archive still
holds data submitted under an earlier reading, and in the register, where the
way a change was made is itself the observation. Where ICES has since
corrected something, the entry says so rather than leaving the defect
standing.

Authored commentary elsewhere in the `imbus` tree is a pointer to where to
look, not evidence. Dates in this article identify a document vintage or an
archive snapshot and nothing else; archive figures were measured against the
full archive on 2026-08-31.

Two of these sources are marked as drafts on their own covers — the pseudo-
category memo, and the 2006 variance-estimation workshop report cited in the
[discrepancy register](#register-of-cross-document-discrepancies). Claims that
rest on them are flagged as such each time.

## The obstacles, in order

The rest of this article is one section per obstacle, ordered by how far it can
move a number you would report, and by how much of it is still unsettled. The
first three account for essentially all of it; the last four are conventions
you need to know but which no longer cost anything once they are handled.

| | Obstacle | What it does to the catch you compute | Where `{obus}` lands |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | [Sub-sampling and the raising factor](#sub-sampling-the-raising-factor-and-datatype) | Sets every number in both tables. Ignore it and a sub-sampled catch is understated by the factor — up to 168× in the worst records in the archive | ICES's index procedure, row by row; `NA`, never an assumed 1, when the factor is missing |
| **2** | [Two routes to a catch total](#two-routes-to-a-catch-total) | Two legitimate totals per haul and species, disagreeing by a whole fish or more in 3.85% of records | Both carried, in separate columns, never averaged; the disagreement measured and flagged per record |
| **3** | [Catch weight](#catch-weight-catcatchwgt) | The one quantity with no arithmetic cross-check in the format. A weight repeated across category codes is added twice | Repeats under `DataType` P collapsed on the main category; the unexplained remainder left summed and flagged |
| **4** | [Length classes and their units](#length-classes-and-their-units) | `LengthClass` holds millimetres and centimetres in one column — a tenfold error on a length if read flat | Resolved once, on reading, into `length_mm`, `length_cm` and `accuracy` |
| **5** | [Record types](#record-types-what-speciesvalidity-means) | Adding up a species across record types counts the same fish twice | `SpeciesValidity` is part of what makes an `HL_summary` row unique |
| **6** | [Haul duration](#haul-duration-and-hourly-rates) | Hourly rates only; 270 hauls have no usable duration | Duration not positive ⇒ `NA`, never `0` and never `Inf` |
| **7** | [Which hauls count](#which-hauls-count) | Whether invalid hauls are in your data at all | `haulval`, with no default — the survey's call, not the package's |
| **8** | [Missing values and `-9`](#missing-values-and-what--9-means) | What an absent value means | Resolved once, upstream, per field; `{obus}` never puts a sentinel back |

Each section says the same three things in the same order: **what ICES's
documents state**, **what the archive actually contains**, and **what `{obus}`
does**. Where the documents conflict, the conflict is registered in the
[discrepancy register](#register-of-cross-document-discrepancies) with an
identifier (D1, D2, …) so it can be cited from elsewhere.

Where a record is affected by any of this, `{obus}` says so per record rather than
in prose alone. `dr_con("hl_flag")` carries one row per affected haul, species
and issue, and `dr_con("hl_flag_code")` explains each code and — importantly —
whether it marks a genuine defect or a documented property of the format:

```{r}
dr_con("hl_flag") |>
  filter(.id == "BITS:2017:4:DK:26HF:TVS:552:42") |>
  left_join(dr_con("hl_flag_code") |> select(code, kind, label), by = "code") |>
  select(Valid_Aphia, code, kind, label)
```

```
  Valid_Aphia        code      kind                          label
       127082 CNT_LEN_DUP   suspect         Duplicated length rows
       126438   CNT_ARITH intrinsic Sub-unit arithmetic difference
       126425   CNT_ARITH intrinsic Sub-unit arithmetic difference
       127150 CNT_LEN_DUP   suspect         Duplicated length rows
```

Most flagged records are `intrinsic` or `property` — arithmetic, or the format
behaving as documented — so filter on `kind` before treating a flag as a
problem. One row per haul, species and issue: a
species with two record types is flagged once, not twice.

## 1. Sub-sampling and the raising factor {#sub-sampling-the-raising-factor-and-datatype}

This is the core of the format, and the part `{obus}` depends on most directly.
It is also the part ICES specified most defensively: the four quantities are
tied together by stated identities — `NoMeas = Sum(HLNoAtLngt)` and
`TotalNo = NoMeas × SubFactor` — so a submission carries its own arithmetic
check, and a consumer can tell a well-formed record from a malformed one
without leaving the file. Almost everything this article is able to say about
where submissions go wrong is said using that redundancy.

### What each field means

| Legacy (current) | Meaning | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| `HLNoAtLngt` (`NumberAtLength`) | **Raw measured count** in the sub-sample, per length class per category. Per-hour for `DataType` C only. | HL row 25: *"Number of measured fish for the length class per category…"*; FAQ Annex I: *"HLNoAtLenght: number of fish measured in the (sub) sample"* |
| `NoMeas` (`SubsampledNumber`) | `Sum(HLNoAtLngt)` over length classes within the category. | HL row 19: *"NoMeas=Sum(HLNoAtLngt)."* |
| `SubFactor` (`SubsamplingFactor`) | The raising factor. ≥ 1, four decimals, per category. For `DataType` S it must be the **compound** of split and species factors. | HL row 20; FAQ Annex I Ex. 1: *"Subfactor = 8\*2 = 16"* |
| `TotalNo` (`TotalNumber`) | **Raised** count = `NoMeas × SubFactor`. Non-mandatory. | FAQ p. 18 (R): *"Make sure that TotalNo = Sum (HLNoAtLngt) x SubFactor"*; FAQ Annex I: *"Total number (TotalNo): subfact\*nomeas"* |

`NumberAtLength`, `SubsampledNumber` and `SubsamplingFactor` are
`Mandatory = Yes` in the current sheet. `TotalNumber` is not.

### The `SubFactor` rule by `DataType`

The `DataType` vocabulary:

| Code | Label |
|---|---|
| `-9` | Invalid hauls |
| `C` | Data calculated as CPUE (number per hour) |
| `P` | Pseudocategory sampling |
| `R` | Data by haul |
| `S` | Sub sampled data |

and the `SubFactor` rule:

> If DataType is C, it should be reported as 1. If DataType is S, it is always
> >1. If DataType is R, the SubFactor is = 1 or >1 for different species
> depending on whether they were subsampled.

So `1` is a specific claim — *this species was not sub-sampled* — and it is
not the same statement as "no factor was supplied", which the format expects
as `-9`.

**`{obus}`:** a missing `SubsamplingFactor` propagates to `NA` for every
`DataType`, including `"R"`. This is a deliberate departure from the DATRAS R
package, which treats `"R"` plus a missing factor as 1. That convention
asserts a fact the submission does not contain: it silently converts "the
raising factor is unknown" into "the catch was fully measured", understating
the raised count whenever the true factor was greater than 1. Following the
format instead costs 24,298 length rows (0.17%), worth 0.003% of the archive's
total `n_haul`, and 98% of them Can-Mar.

### Pseudo category sampling (`P`) and the two-part category identifier

`R` is one sub-sampling rate per species. `P` is size-stratified: several
`CatIdentifier` grades, each sub-sampled separately, under one main category.

Under `P` the `CatIdentifier` is **two digits**: the first is the main
category, the second the sub-category, so main category 1 has sub-categories
`11`, `12`, `13`, and main category 2 has `21`, `22`, `23`. The only document
that describes the convention is the pseudo-category memo [@vaishav2021pseudocat], which is **marked
Draft** and unpublished:

> If datatype is "P" and there is subcategory PRESENT then Catidentifier value
> will be 11, 12,13… 21,21,23…31,32,33..

and, in the same memo:

> Subfactors value are not the same within subcategory
>
> CatCatchweight value is same in each subcategory
>
> Length class are unique in each subcategory

Two-digit `CatIdentifier` codes occur **only** under `DataType` `P` in the
archive: `S` and `C` show zero affected blocks.

**Published ICES documentation for `P` does not exist.** HH row 29 enumerates
the code — *"P (pseudocategory sampling, only used by Scotland)"* — and that is
all. HL row 20 (`SubFactor`) enumerates C, S and R
and is silent on P. HL row 22 (`CatCatchWgt`) says *"For datatype R or S …
For datatype C …"* and is silent on P. The FAQ, which carries every raising
formula in the corpus, contains no occurrence of the word "pseudo" and its
`DataType` paragraph reads *"Data Type can be reported as R …, S …, C …"*. The
FAQ does not know `P` exists.

**`{obus}`:** treats `P` exactly as `R` and `S` — raised count is
`NumberAtLength × SubsamplingFactor`, summed over the rows — because it uses
the row-level formula for every `DataType` and never assumes one category per
species. This is a defensible choice in a documented silence, not an
application of a documented rule.

Note also that the shape `P` describes is submitted under `R` in practice:
34,531 `R` groups carry more than one `SpeciesCategory` each with its own
rate — 2.14% of the 1,616,146 haul × species groups submitted under `R` — across many surveys and back to at least 2009. `{obus}` is unaffected by
that, for the same reason.

### What `{obus}` computes

```
DataType == "C"                 n_haul = NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor * HaulDuration / 60
                                n_hour = NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor
DataType in ("R", "P", "S")     n_haul = NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor
                                n_hour = n_haul / HaulDuration * 60
anything else, including "-9"   n_haul = NA, n_hour = NA
```

`{obus}` invents no arithmetic here. This is the ICES index procedure, step for
step — `Indices_Calculation_Steps_IBTS`, section II:

> d. Raise data from sub sampling to total number per haul by multiplying the
> number at length with the sub sampling factor
>
> e. Sum number at haul by length class over category and sex
>
> f. If data type is not CPUE (C) then NoAthaul=number\*(60/HaulDuration)

`Indices_Calculation_Steps_BITS` states the same three steps independently,
adding *"select valid data … for each category and sex"*. The pseudo-category
memo describes the same two steps again. `dr_HL_length()` is those steps, and
you can do them by hand on any haul and get the published figure back:

```{r}
dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  dr_add_id() |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2020:1:DK:26D4:GOV:11:4", Valid_Aphia == 126425) |>
  summarise(by_hand = sum(NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor))     #> 1606.304

dr_con("HL_length") |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2020:1:DK:26D4:GOV:11:4", Valid_Aphia == 126425) |>
  summarise(published = sum(n_haul))                               #> 1606.304
```

The `DataType` `C` back-multiplication by `HaulDuration/60` — recovering an
absolute per-haul count from a reported rate — is **also** documented by ICES,
in `WKABSENS` 2021 [@ices2021wkabsens], section 3.3 step 17:

> Estimate numbers (Count) / a. If HLNoAgeLngt == NA, use TotalNo and set
> SubFactor = 1 / b. Multiplier = HaulDur/60 if DataType in ("C") / c.
> Multiplier = SubFactor if DataType in ("S","R") / d. Count = HLNoAtLngt \*
> Multiplier

IBTSWG 2022 [@ices2022ibtswg] performs the inverse transform on the
weight field for the same reason: *"CatchWgtraw = (CatchWgtCPUE \* HaulDur) /
60 min"*.

There is one divergence worth naming, and it is not benign. WKABSENS applies
`HaulDur/60` **only** for `C`, with no `SubFactor` term; `{obus}` multiplies by
`SubsamplingFactor` as well. The two agree wherever the format is followed —
and the format is not always followed. **1,832 length rows over 36 BITS hauls
(LT 2008–2016, DK 2018) report `DataType` `C` with `SubFactor > 1`**, reaching
167.94.

Those submissions are shaped like `R` and labelled `C`. Over their 113
haul × species × sex × category groups, `TotalNo` equals
Σ`HLNoAtLngt` in **0** of them, equals Σ`HLNoAtLngt` × `SubFactor` in 102, and
Σ`HLNoAtLngt` equals `NoMeas` in 108 — so `HLNoAtLngt` there is the measured
sub-sample, not an hourly rate, and dropping `SubFactor` understates the catch
by up to 167.94 times.

Three sources decide it against WKABSENS:

- **ICES's own CPUEL product applies both multipliers.** Over 1,721 matched
  cells on those hauls, the median ratio of `CPUE_number_per_hour` to the
  two-multiplier figure is exactly 1.000.
- **The DATRAS R package** [@kristensen2023datraspkg] applied WKABSENS's
  single-multiplier rule until 2023-04-11, then moved to two, over the note
  *"some BITS hauls (all LT and some DK) have dataType C but SubFactor>1 - two
  multipliers needed!"*.
- **The submissions themselves**, as above.

WKABSENS 2021 predates that discovery and
documents behaviour ICES's own production has since superseded — registered as
[D23](#d23), with the CPUEL gear-conversion findings it sits beside at
[D20](#d20)–[D22](#d22).

`{obus}` therefore follows the production behaviour, not the published recipe, and
flags every affected record as `CNT_C_SUBFACTOR_CONFLICT` in
`dr_con("hl_flag")` — because a rule that contradicts an ICES publication
should be visible per record, not buried in a formula. Reproduced by
`data-raw/CHECK_cpuel_multiplier.R`.

## 2. Two routes to a catch total {#two-routes-to-a-catch-total}

There are two independent routes to the same number, and `{obus}` keeps both, in
different tables, named apart on purpose:

| Route | `{obus}` | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Reported | `HL_summary$n_totalnumber` | the recorded `TotalNo` |
| Reconstructed | `sum(HL_length$n_haul)` | raised length frequencies |

`HL_summary` needs the reported route because 16% of its rows are species with
no length data at all, where no length-derived figure exists. `HL_length`
needs the reconstructed route because it is the only one that resolves to a
length class.

Summing `HL_length` reproduces `Σ(NumberAtLength × SubsamplingFactor)` exactly
(1,925,444 groups, zero differing), so nothing is lost by not duplicating it
into `HL_summary`:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dr_con("HL_length") |>
      dplyr::group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity) |>
      dplyr::summarise(n_length = sum(n_haul), .groups = "drop"),
    by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "SpeciesValidity")
  )
```

### The documentation error: `TotalNo=SUM(HLNoAtLngt)`

The current field descriptions contain a sentence that is **false**, and it is
provably false using nothing but ICES's own files.

HL row 17, the field now called `TotalNumber`, still reads
`TotalNo=SUM(HLNoAtLngt).` HL row 19 (`SubsampledNumber`), in the same sheet,
reads `NoMeas=Sum(HLNoAtLngt).` They cannot both be true when
`SubFactor > 1`, because the same sheet also requires
`TotalNo = NoMeas × SubFactor`.

**The Example file inside the same workbook settles it arithmetically.** HL
rows 4–22, `SpecCode` 126417, HH `DataType` `R`:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| The 19 `HLNoAtLngt` values | 2, 2, 5, 6, 16, 28, 22, 32, 21, 28, 31, 14, 12, 6, 4, 3, 3, 1, 1 |
| Their sum | **237** |
| Reported `NoMeas` | **237** — so `NoMeas = Sum(HLNoAtLngt)` is TRUE |
| Reported `TotalNo` | **9766.059** — so `TotalNo = SUM(HLNoAtLngt)` is FALSE, by a factor of 41 |
| Reported `SubFactor` | **41.207**, and 237 × 41.207 = **9766.059** exactly |

So `TotalNo = Sum(HLNoAtLngt) × SubFactor` is the live rule, and the workbook
settles the question against its own sentence. Three further ICES statements
agree with the example: FAQ p. 18's
`DataType` R block, FAQ Annex I's bullet list, and both FAQ worked examples
(Ex. 1, a `DataType` S case: *"Nomeas = ∑(Hlnoat length) = 50 / Subfactor =
8\*2 = 16 / TotalNo = nomeas \* Subfactor = 50\*16 = 800"*).

**It is a leftover from an edit that otherwise worked.** These four
descriptions — `TotalNo`, `NoMeas`, `HLNoAtLngt` and `CatCatchWgt` — were
rewritten together in a review ICES ran on exactly this problem. IBTSWG 2024
[@ices2025ibtswg] §3.3 minutes the intersessional group that met to *"review
the field specifications of the DATRAS format, of which the ambiguity had
likely led to some of the documented issues"*, with *"particular attention … to
the clarification and harmonisation of specifications for the ambiguous fields
… CatCatchWgt, TotalNo, NoMeas and HlNoAtLngt, in particular the description of
their aggregation levels"*; the recommendations went through WGDG and into the
workbook, whose `General Notes` list all four fields under *"Improved
descriptions"*. That review is why the four descriptions now agree on the
record key at all ([what makes a row unique](#what-makes-a-row-unique)). The formula
fragment `TotalNo=SUM(HLNoAtLngt).` simply survived the pass that fixed the
sentence around it.

The fragment is additionally **true for `DataType` C only**, where `SubFactor`
is 1 and both sides are per-hour — FAQ p. 19 states it for C explicitly —
which is very likely why it outlived that review for R, S and P.

### Is there a reading under which `{obus}` is wrong?

Two, and both are dead.

**Reading 1 — "don't raise at all."** Take `TotalNo=SUM(HLNoAtLngt)`
literally: the length sum needs no `SubFactor`, and `{obus}` over-raises. Refuted
by the Example file, by the FAQ's R rule, by Annex I, and by both worked
examples — four independent ICES sources against one sentence.

**Reading 2 — "the length rows are already raised, so `{obus}` double-raises."**
Not a live reading, but worth answering, because it is what the descriptions
said before that review (`HLNoAtLngt=NoMeas*Subfactor`) and it survives in code
built against them. Refuted by the Example file, which sat unchanged in those
very same workbooks and shows `Sum(HLNoAtLngt) = NoMeas = 237`, not 9766. The
formula was also incoherent on its face — a per-row identity that can only hold
when there is exactly one length class — and the current descriptions no longer
carry it.

### Two submitter conventions for `TotalNo`'s scope

Registered as [D4](#d4).

The documents agree with each other now. They did not always, and the archive
is older than the agreement:

| Convention | Where it is stated |
|---|---|
| per species × sex × devstage × category | the current field descriptions, and FAQ p. 18 — *"the total number of fish of one species, sex, and category in the given haul"* |
| haul × species, repeated identically on every sex and category row | the field descriptions as they stood before the harmonisation [@ices2023fielddesc] — *"Total number of specimens in the haul for the species."* |

Both conventions are present in the archive, and **nothing in the record marks
which one a given row follows.** So this is neither `{obus}` deviating from a
documented rule nor a documentary dispute a closer reading can settle: it is a
rule clarified after much of the data was submitted, with no flag in the data
saying which side of the clarification a row falls on. It has to be resolved
per group, arithmetically — which is what `dr_HL_summary()` does below.

### How `{obus}` resolves a repeated `TotalNo` {#how-obus-deduplicates-totalno}

`dr_HL_summary()` resolves the ambiguity per group rather than by picking one
convention globally:

1. **Reconcile.** For each sub-record — haul, species, category, record type,
   sex and development stage — compare its **own** reported `TotalNo` against
   what its **own** length rows raise to. A sub-record that reconciles (within
   half a fish) is *trusted* and counted on its own.
2. **Fall back.** Sub-records that do not reconcile — or that have no length
   rows to check against, such as a bulk-weighed category — are reduced to
   their distinct `TotalNo` values, ignoring sex and category, and leaving out
   any value a reconciling sub-record has already claimed, so nothing is
   counted twice.

Both branches are needed. A plain `distinct()` on the value alone gets the
common cases right but collapses two genuinely different sexes that happen to
report the same small number: a real BITS haul with F (own total 2), M (own
total 1) and unsexed (own total 1, coincidentally equal to M's) has a true
total of 4, and `distinct()`-on-value-alone gives 3.

`SpeciesCategory` is excluded from the *fallback* key because some surveys
report two categories sharing one identical, non-reconciling `TotalNo` — in
practice entirely NS-IBTS, SCOROC and SCOWCGFS, always the category pair
`"11"`+`"12"`, 1,430 haul × species groups archive-wide (0.062%). That value is the
species-level total for both strata together, so keeping `SpeciesCategory` in
the two categories separate adds it once per category and inflates the total by close to
2×. The *trusted* branch still credits any category whose own data genuinely
reconciles.

`DevelopmentStage` is in the key because the ICES record key puts it there.
Archive-wide it moves almost nothing: 289 groups span more than one
`DevStage`, 21 of them with colliding `TotalNo`, worth +29 fish out of
1,443,326,029. Correct by the book and invisible in practice.

**How well the hybrid does, measured.** On the closest reproducible
population — 1,150 groups sharing one `TotalNo` across two-digit categories,
all `DataType` P — `{obus}` returns 3,252,517 against an independent length sum of
3,252,507. A naive sum that treats each `SpeciesCategory` as its own total gives
6,584,935, i.e. **2.02× too high**; that half of the comparison is
established. A blanket collapse that always drops `SpeciesSex` and `SpeciesCategory`
gives 3,252,503 on the same population — within 0.0004% of `{obus}`. So the
hybrid's advantage over the naive route is demonstrated; its advantage over a
blanket collapse is **not established** on the archive as it stands, and
should not be claimed.

### Where the two routes disagree

Comparison must be made **in submission units**. For `DataType == "C"` both
sides are scaled by `HaulDuration/60`, which turns whole fish into fractions:
a genuine one-fish disagreement in a 30-minute haul appears as 0.5 and slips
under any sub-unit tolerance. Divide the scaling out first; then a gap is in
fish.

Of 1,912,556 comparable groups:

| Gap, in submission units | Groups | Share | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exactly zero | 1,702,315 | 89.01% | reconciles |
| Less than one fish | 136,645 | 7.14% | **arithmetic — not a data issue** |
| One or more whole fish | 73,596 | **3.85%** | real |

The sub-fish population is arithmetic and nothing else: a non-integer raising
factor applied to integer counts cannot give an integer, and the reported
`TotalNo` is an integer. It carries no information about the data and is
excluded from everything below. Reporting it as part of a "disagreement rate"
only inflates the number. Independent reproductions of the whole comparison
land at 1,912,200–1,912,600 comparable groups, 88.3–89.0% exact, and
73,400–74,250 whole-fish. Bucket counts below move further than that — the
1-fish band has ranged over ~900 groups across reproductions — so read the
shares, which are stable to a few tenths of a percent, rather than the counts.

**Direction, by gap size** (non-Can-Mar; Can-Mar is separated because it is a
single suspected event):

| Gap | Groups | `TotalNo` higher |
|---|---|---|
| 1 fish | 21,664 | 48.3% |
| 2 fish | 9,965 | 53.6% |
| 3–5 | 7,229 | 61.8% |
| 6–10 | 2,454 | **86.3%** |
| 11–50 | 1,416 | **81.6%** |
| >50 | 441 | 37.2% |

Small gaps are near-symmetric; middling gaps point one way more than four
times in five; and above 50 fish the direction **flips**, so the length sum is
the higher side in 62.8% of that tail. The obvious summary statistic is
actively misleading here: the overall direction split is 55/45, which looks
like noise and is not — it is a symmetric population, a strongly directional
one, and a reversed tail added together.

### What explains the disagreement

The whole-fish residual breaks down as follows. Established causes and
labelled hypotheses are marked.

| Population | Groups | Cause | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Can-Mar | 31,047 | — | **hypothesis only** (see below) |
| 1–2 fish, five directional pockets | 9,452 of ~38,700 | Can-Mar, non-unit `SubFactor`, PT-IBTS / FR-CGFS, BTS, EVHOE | established |
| 1–2 fish, remainder | 29,145 | genuine symmetric noise — 50.27% one way, 95% CI [49.69–50.85], p = 0.36 | established |
| 6–50 fish | 2,738 of 3,885 | `DataType` C with a non-integer raising factor, rounded by the submitter **per length row** | established |
| 6–50 fish | 618 | `DataType` C, `NoMeas` missing — same family by `DataType` and direction | probable |
| 6–50 fish | 112 | exact 2× / 3× integer-ratio scaling error | established |
| 6–50 fish | 116 | non-C, `NoMeas` arbitrates one side as the outlier | established |
| 6–50 fish | 301 | non-C where neither identity reconciles; C with integer factor | **unexplained** |
| >50 fish | 214 of 443 | [duplicated length series](#duplicated-length-series) | established |
| >50 fish | 21+ of 64 | `SubFactor` reported as a rounded integer, over-raising `TotalNo` | established |
| >50 fish | 165 `TotalNo`-higher + 43 length-higher | — | **unexplained** |

(The 6–50 and >50 sub-counts were computed on an independent reproduction of
the same buckets, with denominators 3,885 and 443, which is why they do not
sum to the 3,891 and 462 in the direction table above.)

**The strongest single result.** Define `F = TotalNo / NoMeas` in submission
units — the whole multiplier the submitter actually used. Over 404,833
non-Can-Mar `DataType` C groups:

| `F` | Groups | Whole-fish disagreement rate |
|---|---|---|
| Integer | 298,653 | **0.16%** |
| Non-integer | 106,180 | **29.35%** |

A relative risk of **187×**, using no reconstruction whatsoever. Haul-duration
divisibility alone does not produce it: even where `60 %% HaulDuration == 0`,
the rate is 32.83% with a non-integer factor against 0.14% with an integer
one.

The mechanism is reconstructible. `m_i = round(NumberAtLength_i / F)` recovers
the submitter's raw integer counts, and those `m_i` sum **exactly** to the
independently reported `NoMeas` in 87–96% of groups. So the submitter computed
`NumberAtLength = round(m_i × F)` row by row while computing
`TotalNo = F × Σm_i` once. The per-row residuals do not cancel; their sum is
the gap. **The fish are missing from the submitted file before `{obus}` ever reads
it.**

**The 1–2 fish and 6–50 fish populations are one mechanism, not two.** Inside
the 6–50 bucket, classified by the provider's rounding regime (n = 2,393
classifiable): symmetric rounders (n = 326) are 26.1% `TotalNo`-higher; mixed
(n = 363) 89.5%; **truncators — providers flooring more than 90% of rows
(n = 1,704) — 99.9%**. Truncating providers, as a share of their own groups:
PT-IBTS 46.1%, FR-WCGFS 30.4%, FR-CGFS 15.1%, BITS 10.8%, NS-IBTS 9.6%,
SE-SOUND 4.9%. Magnitude scales with the number of occupied length classes;
direction is set by floor-versus-round-half. Catch size is not a driver
(median |gap| = 0.02 in every `TotalNo` size class from under 50 to over
5,000).

### Can-Mar, unexplained

Can-Mar alone contributes 31,047 whole-fish groups — **41.8% of the residual**.
The shape is distinctive: median gap **13 fish**, **98%** with `TotalNo` the
higher side, and **88.2%** carrying `SubsamplingFactor == 1`. Two mechanisms
fit — a raising factor lost in a provider-side conversion, or fish counted into
`TotalNo` that never entered a length row — and nothing yet separates them, so
neither is claimed here. One thing is ruled out: a per-length-class half-fish
truncation, since `gap / n_length_classes` has median 1.000 (Q1 0.333,
Q3 3.333) rather than 0.5, far too dispersed for any per-class mechanism.

Treat Can-Mar separately, and prefer the reported total there. Both candidate
mechanisms, with the test that would separate them, are in the package's
`TODO.md` under *Open, not resolved*.

### Duplicated length series {#duplicated-length-series}

This is the one place where `{obus}`'s choice of what makes a row unique
measurably moves the number.

Worked case, `BITS:2017:4:DK:26HF:TVS:552:42`, aphia 127082: 38 raw HL rows —
19 under `LenMeasType` `1` and 19 under `LenMeasType` `6`, with the **same 19
`LngtClass` values, the same 19 `HLNoAtLngt` values, the same `SubFactor` 1,
the same `NoMeas` 57, the same `TotalNo` 57, and the same `CatCatchWgt`
4500**. One length series written twice under two measurement-type codes.

`dr_HL_length()` treats `LengthType` and `DevelopmentStage` as part of what
makes a row unique, and therefore adds both copies together (114); the
`TotalNo` route reports them once (57). Ratio exactly 2.000.

Archive-wide, **428 of 1,925,444 records (0.022%)** shrink if identical length
rows — same sex, category, length code, length class, number and factor — are
counted once. **426 of those 428 land in the whole-fish
gap class**, and 221 of them in the >50 band. In the units `HL_length`
actually carries — `n_haul`, haul-scaled for `DataType` C — the duplicated
copies are worth **195,059 of the 394,993 raised fish in those groups**. (In
submission units, i.e. before the `DataType` C scaling, the same excess is
228,904; the two figures must not be interchanged.)

By survey:

| Survey | Groups |
|---|---|
| BITS | 124 |
| NSSS | 97 |
| PT-IBTS | 93 |
| BTS | 80 |
| NS-IBTS | 22 |
| SCOWCGFS | 7 |
| DYFS | 4 |
| FR-CGFS | 1 |

This is why NSSS is 100% length-sum-higher in the >50 tail (69 of 69 groups
resolved) and PT-IBTS 95%.

**Hypothesis: these are coding artefacts, not two real measurement
conventions.** `LenMeasType` codes such as `1` and `6` should be genuinely
different length definitions, so the *same fish* measured both ways would give
*different* `LngtClass` values. The observed series are identical in
`LngtClass` **and** `HLNoAtLngt` **and** `NoMeas` **and** `TotalNo` **and**
`CatCatchWgt`, which is physically impossible under a genuine dual-measurement
reading. *What would settle it:* resolving ICES vocabulary `ref=1392` and
confirming the codes are non-convertible measurement definitions, plus
confirming 100% series identity across all 428 groups.

Keeping `LengthType` distinct is justified by the 885 records that genuinely
split on it; these 428 are the subset where the two series are copies. `{obus}`
does not merge them.

### What is *not* responsible

Negative results worth recording, because each was a plausible suspect:

| Suspect | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Rows `{obus}` drops (`LengthClass` `NA`, `NumberAtLength == 0`) | Present in only 97 of 3,885 target groups, and in **zero** of them does the gap equal the raised value on the dropped rows. Dead. |
| `LngtCode` / `LngtClass` mis-binning | Enriched (2.57% against a 0.11% baseline) but mechanically inert — re-binning cannot change a sum taken over all lengths. Refuted. |
| `{obus}`'s own way of resolving repeats | Multi-sex groups are *less* common in the target bucket (4.94%) than among exactly-agreeing groups (8.69%). Multi-devstage 2.50% against 0.02%; `SpecVal ≠ 1` 1.57% against 5.53%. Not the driver. |

## 3. Catch weight {#catch-weight-catcatchwgt}

`SpeciesCategoryWeight` (legacy `CatCatchWgt`) is the catch weight of one
species category, in whole grams. It is the weaker of the two paths through
this article, for one structural reason: the format gives it **no arithmetic
cross-check**. Numbers have `TotalNo = NoMeas × SubFactor`, so a submission can
be tested against itself. A weight can only be compared with other weights.

### Which weights are the same weight

The problem to solve is that one weight is written onto many rows. A species
category weighed once appears again on every sex row, every development-stage
row and every length row of that category, and adding the column up multiplies
the catch by however many rows the submitter happened to write.

`{obus}` therefore reduces to the distinct weights per species category before
summing — dropping `SpeciesSex` and `DevelopmentStage` from what counts as a
separate weight, and keeping the category:

```
distinct(.id, Valid_Aphia, <category>, SpeciesValidity, SpeciesCategoryWeight)
```

The reason for dropping sex is measured, not assumed: DATRAS repeats one weight
across a species' sex rows whatever the specification says — confirmed as a
threefold inflation on a real NS-IBTS haul with three sex groups in one
category — while genuinely separate per-sex weights, which some programmes do
record, differ from each other and are kept and summed.

**The documents cut both ways on this.** The current field descriptions put
both sex and devstage in `SpeciesCategoryWeight`'s key — ICES's own wording,
not field names. Against that, FAQ p. 19 scopes the field for `DataType` C as *"the total catch
weight per species per haul, raised to one hour of hauling"* — no sex, no
category. Whether dropping sex costs anything where two genuinely separate per-sex
weights happen to be numerically **equal** is **untested**: such a pair is
indistinguishable from one weight written twice. The diagnostic
that would settle it is mean weight per fish, `w_haul / n_haul`, compared
against single-sex groups of the same species and year; a clean ~0.5 offset
would confirm a loss, no offset would confirm the equal weights were genuine
repeats.

### The same weight written on two category codes

Keeping the category is right when two categories are two separately weighed
parts of the catch. It is wrong when the same weight has simply been written on
two codes — and under **pseudo-category sampling (`DataType` P) that is the
documented convention**, not an error. The pseudo-category memo states
*"CatCatchweight value is same in each subcategory"*, and the archive agrees:
of 1,464 P main categories with more than one sub-category, **1,456 (99.5%)
carry a single identical weight**. The structural reason is in the sampling
itself — under P the raising factor *is* category weight divided by sample
weight, so the category weight must appear on every sub-category row of that
category.

**`{obus}` therefore collapses P weights on the main category**, not on the
reported code. Under P the `CatIdentifier` is two digits, the first being the
main category, so `11`, `12` and `13` are one weighing and not three. Take the
worked case that used to be wrong:

```{r}
dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  dr_add_id() |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2016:1:GB-SCT:748S:GOV:12:12", Valid_Aphia == 126437) |>
  distinct(SpeciesCategory, TotalNumber, SpeciesCategoryWeight)
```

```
  SpeciesCategory TotalNumber SpeciesCategoryWeight
               11         613                105300
               12         613                105300
```

Both sub-categories carry 105,300 g, which is one catch weighed once.
`HL_summary` returns it once:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2016:1:GB-SCT:748S:GOV:12:12", Valid_Aphia == 126437) |>
  select(n_totalnumber, w_haul)                       #> 613, 105300
```

Left uncollapsed this one haul would report 210,600 g for a 105,300 g catch,
and archive-wide the P repeats were worth 410,122,351 g — close to 29% of all
`DataType` P weight mass, because sub-category sampling is used precisely on
the big catches. The records are still marked, as `WGT_CAT_REPEAT_P` in
`dr_con("hl_flag")`, with `kind` `property`: the flag records that the
submission carries the repetition, not that the published weight is wrong.

**What is deliberately not collapsed.** The same shape occurs under `DataType`
R, where ICES documents no sub-category convention at all, and there the cause
is not established: of 209 such records, 135 are a single vessel and year
(NS-IBTS 2025 Q3, GB, platform 74E9), and among those where `TotalNumber` also
differs some ties look implausible (two categories both at exactly 9,992 g) and
some entirely plausible (two tiny catches both at 12 g). Collapsing them would
assert a convention no document states, so `{obus}` sums them and flags them
`WGT_CAT_REPEAT_R`, `kind` `unexplained`. A further 36 P records share one
weight *across* main categories, which the memo does not describe either.

Together those are the whole of the remaining excess. Set the published
`w_haul` against the alternative of collapsing every repeated weight whatever
the `DataType`:

```{r}
published <- dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity) |>
  summarise(w_pub = sum(w_haul, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

collapsed <- dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  dr_add_id() |>
  inner_join(dr_con_raw("HH") |> dr_add_id() |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(DataType != "C") |>
  distinct(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, SpeciesCategoryWeight, DataType) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, DataType) |>
  summarise(w_alt = sum(SpeciesCategoryWeight, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

published |>
  inner_join(collapsed, by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "SpeciesValidity")) |>
  filter(w_pub > w_alt + 0.5) |>
  group_by(DataType) |>
  summarise(records = n(), excess_g = sum(w_pub - w_alt))
```

```
  DataType records excess_g
         R     211 18338213
         P      36   175550
```

**18,513,763 g in all — 0.080% of the archive's `w_haul` mass** of
23,263,243,838 g. Before the P collapse the same comparison returned
428,460,512 g, or 1.84%. The flag table marks 1,491 P and 209 R records.

**The numbers are unaffected either way.** For all 1,491 P repeated-weight
records the underlying length frequencies **differ**, so the mechanism that
repeats a weight never touches `n_haul`. Conversely the weight path ignores
`DevelopmentStage` and `LengthType`, so the [duplicated length
series](#duplicated-length-series) that inflate `n_haul` in 428 records cannot
inflate `w_haul` there. The two affected sets are expected to be disjoint; that
has **not been computed**, and a non-empty result would be a new finding.

`w_haul` is `NA`, not `0`, for a species with no recorded weight at all —
672,076 `HL_summary` rows archive-wide, which is 671,937 haul × species
combinations once the record types are counted once, and that is the number
flagged `WGT_NONE`. Not weighed is not weighed nothing.

### A cross-check that exists but is not stated in words

**A hypothesis worth testing.** The Example file establishes,
arithmetically and exactly, that `SubFactor = CatCatchWgt / SubWgt`:
343666 / 8340 = 41.206954…, reported as **41.207**, and 237 × 41.207 =
9766.059 exactly — the example reproduces only from the *rounded* factor.

The arithmetic is a fact of the file. **The generalisation is a hypothesis: no
ICES document states this identity in words anywhere.** If it holds generally,
the weight path has the exact analogue of `TotalNo = NoMeas × SubFactor`, and
becomes checkable. *What would settle it:* over all HL rows with `SubWgt`,
`CatCatchWgt` and `SubFactor` populated, compute the ratio
`CatCatchWgt / SubWgt` and compare it to the reported factor, stratified by survey × year ×
`DataType`. High agreement means the factor is weight-derived and the weight
fields are mutually consistent; agreement in some provider blocks only would
itself identify which providers derive the factor by weight and which by
number; systematic failure would mean one of the three fields is being written
with a different meaning.

The same observation may close the sub-one-fish count population
documentarily: a submitter deriving `TotalNo` from the **unrounded** factor
while writing the rounded four-decimal factor into the rows produces a forced
sub-fish gap (237 × 41.206954 = 9766.048 against the reported 9766.059). That
too is a hypothesis, testable the same way.

### Other weight questions, all open

None of these is a finding, and they share one instrument that has not been
built: **mean weight per fish, `w_haul / n_haul`, stratified by species**.
That quantity is biologically bounded within roughly an order of magnitude, so
any mechanism that scales weight without scaling number leaves a
self-normalising signature — which is what makes the whole family testable at
once.

Two of them could move a published figure:

- **`DataType` C weight standardisation.** HL row 22 makes `CatCatchWgt` for C
  a rate — *"For datatype C, values should be standardised to 60 minutes"*. If
  `w_haul` treats those weights as per-haul while `n_haul` back-multiplies C
  numbers by `HaulDuration/60`, then `w_haul / n_haul` for C is wrong by
  `60 / HaulDuration`. That would touch roughly a third of the archive, against
  the 0.08% of weight mass the repeated weights above account for. Untested.
- **Sex excluded from the weight key.** Two genuinely separate per-sex weights
  that happen to be numerically equal are indistinguishable from one weight
  written twice, and would be counted once. Untested ([D11](#d11)).

The remainder — swapped `SubWgt`/`CatCatchWgt`, unit errors in a grams field
(a realised case is minuted in IBTSWG 2025 Table 3.8.1), the P blocks sharing a
weight across main categories, the R duplicates, and the groups carrying weight
with no number at all — are recorded with their tests in the package's
`TODO.md` under *Open, not resolved*.

## 4. Length classes and their units {#length-classes-and-their-units}

`LengthCode` (legacy `LngtCode`) declares the resolution, and `LengthClass`
(legacy `LngtClass`) **carries mixed units within one column**. Both the units
specification and the format sheet say so:

> LngtClass — Length class in mm for mm and 1/2-cm classes, in cm for cm
> classes

**`{obus}`** resolves this once, at read time, into three columns:

| `LengthCode` | Unit of `LengthClass` | `length_mm` | `length_cm` | `accuracy` (cm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `.` | mm | `LengthClass` | `LengthClass / 10` | 0.1 |
| `0` | mm (½-cm classes) | `LengthClass` | `LengthClass / 10` | 0.5 |
| `1` | cm | `LengthClass * 10` | `LengthClass` | 1 |
| `2` | cm (2-cm classes) | `LengthClass * 10` | `LengthClass` | 2 |
| `5` | cm (5-cm classes) | `LengthClass * 10` | `LengthClass` | 5 |
| anything else, or `-9` | — | `NA` | `NA` | `NA` |

`accuracy` is part of what makes a row unique, not an annotation: a 1-cm and a
5-cm series for the same species in the same haul are different observations.

The mixing is plain in the data. `LengthClass` runs to 11,930 under the
millimetre code and stops at 900 under the centimetre one — the same column,
two units:

```{r}
dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  group_by(LengthCode) |>
  summarise(rows = n(),
            smallest = min(LengthClass, na.rm = TRUE),
            largest  = max(LengthClass, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(rows))
```

```
  LengthCode    rows smallest largest
           1 8322123        0     900     # centimetres
           . 4470490        0   11930     # millimetres
           0 1248295        0    1300     # millimetres, half-cm classes
        <NA>  377784       NA      NA
           5    5079       60     160     # centimetres, 5-cm classes
```

ICES does publish the vocabularies themselves, at `vocab.ices.dk`, and the
`Survey` description links to its own list directly. What is missing is the
pointer: the workbook's `Vocab` column — which should name the vocabulary that
enumerates each coded field — is populated in exactly **one cell** across all
three unaggregated sheets (CA `PreservationMethod`). It is empty for
`DataType`, `SpeciesValidity`, `SpeciesSex`, `LengthCode`, `DevelopmentStage`
and `LengthType`: 0 of 71 HH rows and 0 of 27 HL rows. So the code values in
the tables above are read from prose and from the data, not from a
machine-readable list the format points at ([D17](#d17)).

## 5. Record types: what `SpeciesValidity` means {#record-types-what-speciesvalidity-means}

The field descriptions call `SpeciesValidity` (legacy `SpecVal`) the

> Validity of species records, e.g. to specify if species has only been
> counted, measured, weighed, etc.

The codes describe *what data is present*, not how good it is:

| Code | What is present |
|---|---|
| `1` | Lengths, numbers and weights |
| `4` | Total number only |
| `5` | Presence / absence |
| `6` | Weight only |
| `7` | Numbers and weights, no lengths |

There is no ordering, so there is no "most valid" code to collapse to, and the
format deliberately allows more than one record type per species per haul.

**`{obus}`:** `SpeciesValidity` is part of what makes an `HL_summary` row unique.
1,219 haul × species records (0.05% of 2,290,203) carry more than one record
type; the commonest pairs are `{1,5}` and `{4,7}`:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  count(.id, Valid_Aphia) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  count()                                   #> 1219
```
 Filtering to a single code makes `.id` × `Valid_Aphia`
exactly unique (verified at codes `"1"`, `"4"`, `"5"` and `"7"`). Aggregating
over `.id` × `Valid_Aphia` without also grouping on `SpeciesValidity` mixes record
types and double-counts.

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  dplyr::filter(SpeciesValidity == "1")   # the usual starting point
```

**The documents disagree on which codes are valid, and this is
survey-specific.** `Indices_Calculation_Steps_BITS` [@ices2013bitsindices] states a rule —

> CPUE values are only estimated for hauls with validity codes "V" and "N" and
> for species with species validity code "SpecValCode" 1 or NULL

— and its Annex 2 repeats `SpecValCode = 1 OR NULL`, so BITS treats *missing*
